title: Mafia connections and a record label owner's trouble
summary: He was never strong-armed; mobsters' girlfriends occasionally recorded, and one label owner who took Marcello money was caught and beaten.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Did you ever get, did you ever get the mafia connection?
No, no, no, no. And the reason, the reason for it is because, you know, I knew some of the minor hoods, you know.
They went about their business. They weren't interested in me.

Now, now and then one of them would have a girlfriend or somebody wanted to sing, you know, and they'd do a session with them. I probably did a dozen sessions over the years with some nightclub owner's girlfriend, you know.
Somebody's trying to get in bed with someone.

Yeah. Oh, no. I don't think these guys, you had to get in bed first before you got to session. But, you know, but they're usually terrible singers, you know. And they'd probably use the club band if I couldn't talk them into using, you know, a studio group.
I don't know if any of those had ever amounted. I can't even remember.

Oh, no, no. The only time I had a problem, there was a guy who got money from the Marcellos to start a record company. And I was on the big studio on Governor Nichols, 521. And he did some sessions and all that. Nothing came of him.
But he also spent a lot. He bought himself a car and he had a girlfriend and all that with their money.
And he turned up missing, you know. They caught him in Alabama and broke his legs. I don't know if I want that on the thing, but I guess it's all right.
Wait a minute. I don't think you're tarnishing Marcellos.
No, no, no, no. No. That's what you just did. Literally, he broke his legs.
Yeah, that's right. Yeah. That was my cousin he was in tomato business with.
